newsitem.title: UK: London precious metals weaker, ignore U.S. jobs.
newsitem.headline: London precious metals weaker, ignore U.S. jobs.

text.p: Precious metals were weaker on Friday and looked vulnerable to further easing due to a lack of buying interest, dealers said.
The gold market shrugged off stronger-than-expected U.S. jobs data, despite potentially bullish concerns that inflation could be on the rise.
It closed at $385.55 an ounce, down $0.80 from Thursday's London finish, but little changed from the day's opening price.
"Clearly if we start getting more evidence of the potential for rising inflation, we'll get more people interested in gold. But it's too early," said analyst Kevin Crisp of JP Morgan.

But some dealers said gold's brief dip lower just after the jobs data meant the market though a strong U.S. economy was more likely to lead to higher interest rates -- a potentially bearish factor for gold.
U.S. non-farm payrolls rose 250,000 from a gain of 228,000 the previous month. The unemployment rate was 5.1 percent, the lowerst since March 1989, compared to 5.4 previously.
The precious metals complex as a whole was still languishing in the clutches of seasonal doldrums, although demand was expected to pick up later this month.
Gold's failure to rally on the U.S. missile strikes on Iraq earlier this week sparked the bearish mood, dealers said.
Silver was weaker following a sell-off by investment funds overnight, and closed five cents lower at $5.15 an ounce.
"The whole market is threatening to come down. There's just no interest at all," a dealer said.
But silver was expected to encounter buying interest above the psychological $5.00 an ounce level.
Platinum, which has been losing steam regularly over the past five days, finished down $0.80 from Thursday's London close at $393.60 an ounce.
